title: Irrigation as a Crop Buffer and Its Contrasting Hydrologic Impacts Across the Mississippi River Basin Using an Integrated Hydrology‐Crop‐Irrigation Model
content:
Abstract

Irrigation buffers crop production against hydroclimatic variability, but the magnitude of this buffering, the sustainability of the underlying water resources, and its broader hydrologic impacts are rarely quantified together within a single, spatially explicit, process-based framework. We address this gap using an enhanced version of the Community Land Model version 5 (CLM5) in the Mississippi River Basin (MRB), with a novel observation-constrained surface water-groundwater irrigation scheme that improves correlations with observations from r = 0.33–0.79 under the default scheme to r = 0.85–0.96. Results show 2.2%–71.3% less variability in irrigated yields than rainfed yields across the semi-arid High Plains Aquifer (HPA) and humid Mississippi Alluvial Plain (MAP), with the gap between irrigated and rainfed yields up to 222 bushels/acre for corn and 65 bushels/acre for soybean during drought years. Groundwater sustains 90%–99% of this simulated irrigated yield buffer in both HPA and MAP, drawn mainly from deep non-renewable aquifer in the HPA versus seasonally recharging shallow aquifer in the MAP. The environmental trade-offs of this buffering are spatially uneven. Total water storage remains stable in the MAP, whereas the central-southern HPA suffers severe groundwater depletion (−34 to −54 mm/yr). These results highlight how similar irrigation benefits carry vastly different sustainability profiles driven by underlying recharge rates—offering a process-based framework to identify where irrigated agriculture is sustainable versus where it relies on unsustainable groundwater mining.
